newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Yuan seen stable in 1997 but caution warranted.
newsitem.headline: Yuan seen stable in 1997 but caution warranted.

text.p: The Chinese yuan should remain stable in the coming year but companies should be aware that a devaluation is always possible in the case of a foreign exchange shortage, an analyst said on Wednesday.
"The (People's Bank of China) appears committed to maintaining the renminbi's stability," Diane Yowell, director of research at Hongkong Bank China Services Ltd, told a seminar.
The central bank had accumulated foreign exchange reserves of more than US$90 billion to counter the appreciation of the yuan that had accompanied massive capital inflows, she said.
"The government also appears committed to maintaining appropriately tight monetary policy in the face of a lot of pressure. This has been the policy for three years," she noted.

Provided this policy was maintained, the foreign exchange inflow remained strong and there was no big deterioration in the trade balance, "then I think we can say with some safety that the renminbi is going to stay quite stable for the year ahead".
Chinese authorities would keep a tight reign on monetary policy despite heavy pressure to relax, she said.
Unlike the economic leadership of the 1980s, today's policymakers managed the system as a whole instead of just one particular angle of it.

China's plan to allow current account convertibility by the end of 1996 would have a "negligible" impact on the yuan because many domestic firms and foreign investment enterprises already enjoyed adequate access to foreign exchange, Yowell said.
China would continue to control who had access to foreign exchange markets after the rules were relaxed, she said.

Yowell would not speculate on the yuan's movement after 1997. But she warned that any developing country faced the possibility of a foreign exchange shortage. That could mean tighter exchange controls or a devaluation in the future.

"If (Chinese officials) encounter a foreign exchange crisis, you can be sure that (foreign exchange) controls would be considered," she said, adding that such controls would largely affect the yuan rate.
"The other thing they would consider would be allowing the currency to devalue," she said.
Yowell expected China's trade surplus to fall in 1996 and beyond from the US$16.69 billion registered in 1995 as the government reduced subsidies and other support for exporters.
